group.title: Idioms and informal English
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Something disappointing or unlucky.
examples: It’s a {bummer} that the concert is canceled.
wrong: It’s a bummer, so let’s celebrate this great news with a party.

words.meaning: To spend time relaxing with someone.
examples: We usually {hang out} at the park on weekends.
wrong: We hang out by studying alone in a locked room all day.

words.meaning: To watch many episodes of a show in one session.
examples: We plan to {binge-watch} the whole series on Saturday.
wrong: I binge-watched one short episode for two minutes and then stopped.

words.meaning: To relax and stop worrying.
examples: Just {chill out}; there’s plenty of time.
wrong: He told me to chill out, so I ran around in a panic shouting.

words.meaning: To become suddenly very upset or afraid.
examples: Don’t {freak out}; it’s only a small mistake.
wrong: She freaked out by staying perfectly calm and smiling.

words.meaning: To make a mistake or spoil something.
examples: I don’t want to {mess up} the interview.
wrong: I messed up the test, so I got every answer right.

words.meaning: To understand something or find a solution.
examples: I can’t {figure out} how this app works.
wrong: I figured out the answer, so I still have no idea what it is.

words.meaning: To deal with a problem and solve it.
examples: I need to {sort out} my schedule for next week.
wrong: I sorted out the problem, so it became worse and nothing changed.

words.meaning: A decision that is very easy to make.
examples: Taking the free upgrade was a {no-brainer}.
wrong: Choosing between ten difficult plans was a no-brainer that took a month.

words.meaning: A rough estimate.
examples: Give me a {ballpark} figure for the cost.
wrong: A ballpark figure is an exact number measured to the last cent.

words.meaning: To work hard and fast to earn money or succeed.
examples: She has to {hustle} to pay the rent.
wrong: He hustled all day by lying in bed and doing nothing.

words.meaning: The mood or feeling of a place or person.
examples: This café has a really relaxed {vibe}.
wrong: The vibe in the silent, empty room was busy and lively, so everyone felt excited.

words.meaning: Suspicious or not safe.
examples: That website looks {sketchy}; I won’t enter my card.
wrong: I trusted the sketchy shop because everything about it was perfectly safe and clear.

words.meaning: Not reliable; likely to cancel plans.
examples: My friend is {flaky}; he cancels half the time.
wrong: She is so flaky that she has never missed an appointment in ten years.

words.meaning: To complain about very small faults.
examples: Stop trying to {nitpick} every little detail.
wrong: She nitpicked by praising the whole report without noticing any detail.

words.meaning: To do something without preparing.
examples: I didn’t prepare, so I’ll just {wing it}.
wrong: He winged it by rehearsing the speech for ten full days.

words.meaning: To suddenly stop answering someone’s messages.
examples: He {ghosted} me after the second date.
wrong: He ghosted me by replying to every message within a minute.

words.meaning: To feel very embarrassed.
examples: I {cringe} when I hear my old voice recordings.
wrong: I cringe at my old photos because I think they are wonderful and I feel proud of myself.

words.meaning: Annoyed or bitter about something.
examples: He’s still {salty} about losing the game.
wrong: She is salty about her win, so she is overjoyed and not bitter.

words.meaning: Dishonest or not to be trusted.
examples: The deal sounded {shady}, so I said no.
wrong: The shady businessman is known as the most honest man in town.

words.meaning: Extremely tired.
examples: I’m completely {wiped out} after the trip.
wrong: He was wiped out after a long sleep and felt full of energy.

words.meaning: Disappointed or sad.
examples: I’m really {bummed} that you can’t come.
wrong: She was bummed because her team won everything and she felt delighted.

words.meaning: Very excited and happy.
examples: I’m so {stoked} about the trip!
wrong: I am stoked about the canceled trip and feel miserable.

words.meaning: Having no money.
examples: I can’t go out because I’m {broke}.
wrong: He is broke, so he bought a new car with cash.

words.meaning: To go to bed.
examples: I’m exhausted; I’m going to {hit the sack}.
wrong: I hit the sack, so I stayed up all night and never lay down.

words.meaning: To stop working for the day.
examples: We’ve done enough; let’s {call it a day}.
wrong: At nine in the morning they called it a day and went home to sleep for the week, though they had only just started.

words.meaning: To contact someone briefly to share news.
examples: Let’s {touch base} on Friday about the project.
wrong: We touch base by never speaking to each other again.

words.meaning: Ordinary and not special.
examples: It was a {run-of-the-mill} film that I soon forgot.
wrong: The run-of-the-mill hotel was so unique that nobody had ever seen anything like it.

words.meaning: Not yet decided.
examples: Our vacation plans are still {up in the air}.
wrong: Our plans are up in the air, so everything is fixed and settled.

words.meaning: To make people feel more relaxed when they first meet.
examples: A joke can {break the ice} at a party.
wrong: He broke the ice by making everyone feel tense and silent.

words.meaning: Slightly ill.
examples: I’m feeling a bit {under the weather} today.
wrong: He is under the weather, so he runs a marathon and feels great.

words.meaning: To use your influence to get something done.
examples: He {pulled strings} to get her the job.
wrong: He pulled strings by having no friends and no influence.

words.meaning: Official rules that cause delay.
examples: Starting a business involves a lot of {red tape}.
wrong: The red tape made the process fast and simple, with no forms at all.

words.meaning: Something that seems bad but turns out good.
examples: Losing that job was {a blessing in disguise}.
wrong: The lucky win was a blessing in disguise because it clearly seemed wonderful and stayed wonderful.

words.meaning: The final problem that makes you lose patience.
examples: When he forgot again, that was {the last straw}.
wrong: The last straw was the very first small problem of a whole new day.

words.meaning: Very rarely.
examples: We only eat out {once in a blue moon}.
wrong: He visits us once in a blue moon, so he comes every single day.

words.meaning: To do something difficult that you have been avoiding.
examples: I decided to {bite the bullet} and call the dentist.
wrong: She bit the bullet by running away from the hard task for another year.

words.meaning: With very little money.
examples: They built the whole company {on a shoestring}.
wrong: They built the palace on a shoestring with millions of dollars of gold.

words.meaning: To reveal a secret.
examples: Who {spilled the beans} about the surprise party?
wrong: She spilled the beans by keeping the secret perfectly and telling nobody.

words.meaning: To do something in a cheap or careless way.
examples: The builders {cut corners} and the roof leaked.
wrong: A careful builder cuts corners to make everything perfect and safe.
